title: Civilization #20: The Proto-Buddhists of the Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization
description: Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Indus Valley were the three great civilizations of the Bronze Age. What made the Indus Valley Civilization distinct? Why did they decline? What is their legacy? In this lecture to his Chinese high school students, Jiang Xueqin explains that the Indus Valley Civilization (also known as the Harappan Civilization) was mainly a peaceful and egalitarian society, which prospered because of its global trade networks. This civilization had standardized weights and measurements, sophisticated urban planning, as well as private indoor latrines. The dramatic climate change of the 4.2 kiloyear event caused Egypt’s Old Kingdom, Mesopotamia’s Akkadian empire, and the Indus Valley Civilization to decline. The Egyptians left us the Pyramids, the Mesopotamians left us the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the Harappans left us spiritual wealth. From the interaction with the Proto-Indo-Iranians, the Harappan civilization would eventually give birth to Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, which continue to give hope and meaning to billions of people today.

title: "Revisiting the Indus Script: A New Decipherment Perspective Rooted in Cultural, Linguistic, and Symbolic Synthesis"
description: The Indus Script, carved into seals, tablets, pottery, and other artifacts of the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2600–1900 BCE), remains one of the most tantalizing enigmas in world archaeology. Despite over a century of research, it has resisted definitive decipherment, leaving scholars to debate whether it represents a full writing system, a proto-writing stage, or a complex symbolic code. In this research paper, I present a fresh interpretative framework that integrates archaeological evidence, comparative linguistics, ancient cultural symbolism, and computational pattern analysis, offering new insights into the nature, structure, and possible meaning of the Indus Script. My theory challenges the binary view of "script or symbol" by proposing that the Indus glyphs functioned as a multi-layered communication system —a fusion of economic record-keeping, religious symbolism, and clan/territorial identity markers. I argue that previous attempts at decipherment have often failed because they treated the signs as belonging exclusively to one communicative category, rather than as a hybrid system that reflected the intertwined social, economic, and spiritual life of the Harappans. The methodology combines: Contextual Archaeology: Examining findspots, associated artifacts, and spatial distributions to reconstruct socio-economic contexts. Linguistic Parallels: Cross-comparing Indus symbols with early Dravidian, Proto-Elamite, Mesopotamian, and early Brahmi signs to identify possible phonetic or logographic correspondences. Iconographic Analysis: Investigating recurring motifs—such as the unicorn, fish, and plant symbols—not merely as literal representations but as culturally encoded metaphors, possibly linked to astronomy, trade goods, or ritual concepts. Digital Corpus Analytics: Applying frequency analysis, sign order probability, and network mapping to detect grammatical patterns or semantic clustering that manual analysis may overlook. The paper also addresses the sociopolitical dimensions of the script—how its restricted literacy and controlled use on seals could have reinforced elite authority, regulated trade, and maintained cultural cohesion across a vast territory. By correlating glyph groupings with regional artifact types, I propose that some Indus signs may have functioned similarly to heraldic badges or merchant marks, while others carried religious or calendrical .information. Importantly, I explore the symbolic logic underpinning the script. Drawing on comparative mythology, I suggest that the Indus people may have used layered semantic encoding—where one symbol could simultaneously signify a deity, a season, and an economic commodity, depending on context. This polyvalent nature would have allowed the script to operate effectively for different audiences and purposes, from traders to priests. While this work does not claim a complete decipherment, it offers a coherent theoretical model that aligns archaeological, linguistic, and symbolic data into a unified interpretive lens. The findings open pathways for collaborative, interdisciplinary research and invite a reconsideration of the Indus Script not as a failed puzzle but as a sophisticated, multi-functional system worthy of recognition as one of the earliest and most complex semiotic traditions in human history. This research seeks to shift the discourse from isolated decipherment attempts toward a holistic understanding of how the Indus Script functioned within the lived reality of the Harappan world—bridging the gap between silent symbols and the voices of an ancient civilization.

title: Mohenjo Daro History -Lost City of Mohenjo Daro (Documentary)
description: Title: Mohenjo Daro History -Lost City of Mohenjo Daro (Documentary) Mohenjo-daro (means 'Mound of the Dead Men') is an archaeological site in the province of Sindh, Pakistan. Built around 2500 BCE, it was one of the largest settlements of the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation, and one of the world's earliest major cities, contemporaneous with the civilizations of ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Minoan Crete, and Norte Chico. Mohenjo-daro was abandoned in the 19th century BCE as the Indus Valley Civilization declined, and the site was not rediscovered until the 1920s. Significant excavation has since been conducted at the site of the city, which was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980. The site is currently threatened by erosion and improper restoration. Mohenjo-daro is located off the right (west) bank of the lower Indus river in Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan. It lies on a Pleistocene ridge in the flood plain of the Indus, around 28 kilometers (17 mi) from the town of Larkana. Mohenjo-daro was built in the 26th century BCE.  It was one of the largest cities of the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, also known as the Harappan Civilization which developed around 3,000 BCE from the prehistoric Indus culture. At its height, the Indus Civilization spanned much of what is now Pakistan and North India, extending westwards to the Iranian border, south to Gujarat in India and northwards to an outpost in Bactria, with major urban centers at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Mohenjo-daro was the most advanced city of its time, with remarkably sophisticated civil engineering and urban planning. When the Indus civilization went into sudden decline around 1900 BCE, Mohenjo-daro was abandoned. The ruins of the city remained undocumented for around 3,700 years until R. D. Banerji, an officer of the Archaeological Survey of India, visited the site in 1919–20 identifying what he thought to be a Buddhist stupa (150–500 CE) known to be there and finding a flint scraper which convinced him of the site's antiquity. This led to large-scale excavations of Mohenjo-daro led by K. N. Dikshit in 1924–25, and John Marshall in 1925–26.[15] In the 1930s major excavations were conducted at the site under the leadership of Marshall, D. K. Dikshitar and Ernest Mackay. Further excavations were carried out in 1945 by Mortimer Wheeler and his trainee, Ahmad Hasan Dani. The last major series of excavations were conducted in 1964 and 1965 by George F. Dales. After 1965 excavations were banned due to weathering damage to the exposed structures, and the only projects allowed at the site since have been salvage excavations, surface surveys, and conservation projects. In the 1980s, German and Italian survey groups led by Michael Jansen and Maurizio Tosi used less invasive archeological techniques, such as architectural documentation, surface surveys, and localized probing, to gather further information about Mohenjo-daro. A dry core drilling conducted in 2015 by Pakistan's National Fund for Mohenjo-daro revealed that the site is larger than the unearthed area.

title: “Deciphering the Indus Script: Insights into India’s Ancient Civilization”
description: This research paper delves into the mysterious and undeciphered Indus Script of the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, exploring its symbols, patterns, and possible linguistic structures. It examines archaeological discoveries, historical contexts, and comparative analyses with other contemporary writing systems, shedding light on the socio-cultural, economic, and religious life of one of the world’s earliest urban civilizations. The study also discusses challenges in decipherment, modern hypotheses, and the potential insights the script can provide into early human communication, governance, trade, and cultural exchange, highlighting its significance in understanding India’s rich historical heritage and the broader evolution of writing and civilization.

title: A Journey Through Pre-Independence India: Three Epochs in Eight Maps
description: The history of pre-independence India is often categorized into three main periods: the Hindu, Muslim, and British periods. This division, while somewhat simplistic, helps in understanding the major socio-political and cultural shifts that shaped the subcontinent over millennia. Here is a brief overview of each period: Hindu Period Ancient India (c. 3000 BCE — 1200 CE) Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3000–1500 BCE) : The Indus Valley Civilization, also known as the Harappan Civilization, was notable for its sophisticated city planning, with well-laid streets, drainage systems, and large public buildings. The society had a strong emphasis on hygiene and had advanced skills in crafts like bead-making and metallurgy. The decline of this civilization remains a subject of debate among historians, with theories suggesting climate change, invasions, or natural disasters as possible causes. Vedic Period (c. 1500–600 BCE) : This period saw the composition of the Rigveda, which is the oldest of the four Vedas and consists of hymns praising various deities. The Vedic society was initially pastoral but gradually became agrarian. The social structure was based on the varna system, which later evolved into the more rigid caste system. Key texts from this period include the Upanishads, which delve into philosophical concepts like the nature of the self and the universe. Mahajanapadas and Maurya Empire (c. 600–200 BCE) : The formation of large states known as Mahajanapadas marked the beginning of urbanization in the Indian subcontinent. The Magadha kingdom emerged as the most powerful among them. Chandragupta Maurya established the Maurya Empire, with its capital at Pataliputra (modern-day Patna). His grandson, Ashoka, after the bloody Kalinga War, embraced Buddhism and propagated it both within and outside India. Ashoka’s edicts, inscribed on pillars and rocks, provide valuable insights into his reign and policies. Classical Period (c. 200 BCE — 1200 CE) : The Gupta Empire, often referred to as the “Golden Age of India,” saw significant advancements in science, mathematics, astronomy, literature, and art. Scholars like Aryabhata and Kalidasa made substantial contributions during this period. The concept of zero, decimal system, and essential astronomical theories were developed. Temples and cave complexes like those at Ajanta and Ellora were constructed, showcasing exquisite art and architecture. Muslim Period Medieval India (c. 1200–1757 CE) Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) : The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate marked the beginning of Muslim rule in northern India. The Sultanate period saw the construction of iconic structures like the Qutub Minar and the Alai Darwaza. The Sultans introduced Persian culture and administrative practices. Conflicts with regional kingdoms and invasions by Mongols also marked the period. Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646) : The Vijayanagara Empire, founded by Harihara and Bukka, was a significant Hindu kingdom in southern India. The capital, Hampi, was a central cultural and economic hub known for its grand temples and bustling markets. The empire played a crucial role in defending the southern regions from northern invasions and fostering a rich cultural heritage. Mughal Empire (1526–1857) : The Mughal Empire brought about a renaissance in art, culture, and architecture. Akbar’s policy of religious tolerance and administrative innovations, like the Mansabdari system, strengthened the empire. The period saw the construction of architectural marvels like the Fatehpur Sikri complex and the Taj Mahal. The Mughal era also saw significant developments in painting, literature, and gardens. However, the empire began to decline post-Aurangzeb due to internal strife, administrative inefficiencies, and external invasions. British Period Colonial India (1757–1947) Early British Presence and Control : The British East India Company initially came to India for trade but gradually took control of large territories. The Battle of Plassey (1757) and the Battle of Buxar (1764) established British dominance in Bengal, which became the base for further expansion. The Company’s administration imposed high taxes and changed traditional agricultural practices, leading to famines and economic hardship. Company Rule (1757–1858) : The British introduced new land revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement, which had long-term adverse effects on Indian peasants. They also started English education, which created a new class of Western-educated Indians. The economic policies favored British industries at the expense of Indian handicrafts and industries, leading to de-industrialization in many sectors. The Revolt of 1857 : Sparked by various grievances, including the use of animal fat in rifle cartridges, the revolt saw widespread participation from soldiers and civilians alike. The revolt was marked by brutal violence on both sides and ultimately led to the dissolution of the East India Company. The British Crown took direct control, promising reforms and more considerate governance. British Crown Rule (1858–1947) : The British Raj implemented significant infrastructure projects, including the construction of an extensive railway network, telegraph lines, and irrigation projects. However, these developments primarily served British economic interests. The British also introduced legal and administrative reforms, including the Indian Penal Code and the Indian Civil Services. Social reforms, partly influenced by Indian reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy, led to the abolition of practices like sati and the promotion of widow remarriage. Indian National Movement : The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, became the principal platform for nationalist activities. Leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, and later Mahatma Gandhi played pivotal roles. Gandhi’s philosophy of non-violence and civil disobedience galvanized the masses. Key events included: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919). The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22). The Salt March (1930). The Quit India Movement (1942). Parallel to the Congress, revolutionary activities and regional movements also played crucial roles in the struggle for independence. Partition and Independence (1947) : Communal tensions between Hindus and Muslims, fueled by political disagreements and British policies, led to the demand for a separate Muslim state. The Indian National Congress and the Muslim League, led by leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Muhammad Ali Jinnah, eventually agreed to the partition of India. On August 15, 1947, India gained independence, and Pakistan was created. The partition led to one of the largest mass migrations in history and significant violence and suffering. Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2500–1500 BCE) Map Overview:  This map would show the extent of the Indus Valley Civilization, including major sites like Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, and Lothal. Historical Significance:  The Indus Valley Civilization was one of the world’s earliest urban cultures, known for its advanced city planning, architecture, and social organization. It was centered around the Indus River and its tributaries, highlighting a sophisticated and relatively uniform culture across a vast area. Maurya Empire (c. 322–185 BCE) Map Overview:  This map would depict the Maurya Empire at its zenith under Emperor Ashoka, covering almost the entire Indian subcontinent, extending into modern-day Afghanistan and Iran. Historical Significance:  The Maurya Empire was the first to unify most of India under a single administration. Ashoka’s reign is particularly notable for the spread of Buddhism and his efforts to govern by moral principles, as recorded in his rock and pillar edicts. Gupta Empire (c. 320–550 CE) Map Overview:  This map would show the Gupta Empire, often considered a golden age of Indian culture, science, and art, covering much of northern and parts of central India. Historical Significance:  The Gupta period saw significant advancements in mathematics (concept of zero), astronomy, literature (Kalidasa’s works), and art. This era laid the groundwork for many aspects of classical Indian culture. Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) Map Overview:  This map would illustrate the territorial extent of the Delhi Sultanate at its peak, including regions of northern India, parts of the Deccan, and modern-day Pakistan and Bangladesh. Historical Significance:  The Delhi Sultanate introduced significant Persian cultural and administrative practices and was a period of substantial Islamic influence in northern India. It paved the way for the cultural syncretism that would define the subcontinent. Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646) Map Overview:  This map would show the extent of the Vijayanagara Empire in southern India, including its capital, Hampi. Historical Significance:  The Vijayanagara Empire was a prominent Hindu kingdom that resisted northern invasions and became a center of trade, culture, and learning. Its impressive architecture and vibrant cultural life are well-documented through the ruins at Hampi. Mughal Empire (1526–1707) Map Overview:  This map would depict the Mughal Empire at its height under Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan, covering most of the Indian subcontinent. Historical Significance:  The Mughal Empire is renowned for its contributions to art, architecture (Taj Mahal), and culture. It established a centralized administrative system and promoted a composite culture blending Persian, Indian, and various local traditions. British India (1858–1947) Map Overview:  This map would show British India, highlighting the extent of British control, including princely states and directly administered territories. Historical Significance:  British rule brought significant infrastructural changes, such as railways, telegraph, and modern education. However, it also led to economic exploitation and widespread social upheaval. The map would illustrate the geopolitical divisions that led to the independence movement and eventual partition. Partition and Independence (1947) Map Overview:  This map would show the newly independent states of India and Pakistan following the partition, with borders dividing the Punjab and Bengal regions. Historical Significance:  The partition of 1947 resulted in massive demographic shifts, communal violence, and the creation of two sovereign states, India and Pakistan. This event marked the end of British colonial rule and the beginning of a new chapter in the subcontinent’s history.

title: Echoes of Bharat: Chronicles of Ancient India
description: Echoes of Bharat: Chronicles of Ancient India takes you on an immersive journey through one of the world’s oldest and most enduring civilizations. From the meticulously planned cities of the Indus Valley to the philosophical depths of the Vedic age, from the political brilliance of the Mauryan Empire to the cultural flowering of the Gupta period, this book unravels the many layers of India’s ancient past. Drawing on archaeological discoveries, ancient texts, inscriptions, and modern research, the narrative blends history with culture, philosophy, science, and art—revealing how India’s ancestors built cities, pioneered innovations, developed systems of governance, and nurtured values that still resonate today. More than a record of events, this work is a tapestry of stories—of kings and queens, sages and scholars, warriors and common people—whose contributions shaped the soul of Bharat. It celebrates the timeless heritage, unity in diversity, and intellectual brilliance that made ancient India a cradle of civilization. Whether you are a student, history enthusiast, or simply curious about India’s roots, Echoes of Bharat offers a rich, engaging, and inspiring exploration of a legacy that continues to guide the present and illuminate the future.

title: Vinca Tablets C. 5, 500 BC Earliest Example Of Wr
description:
The Origin of Writing: While it is still generally considered that writing emerged 'independently in at least three different places - Egypt, Mesopotamia and Harappa between 3,500 BC and 3,100 BC' , we have until recently had little understanding of how and why this happened. The discovery of the Vinca script and (mother) culture c. 5,500 - 3,500 BC, has offered a possible clue as to this question, but more importantly, symbols in the Vinca script can be seen to have roots that trace back as early as Palaeolithic times. 

We are now aware of the Vinca (Mother) culture which existed in Eastern Europe around 5,500 - 4,500 BC.  The earliest examples of Vinca script (such as the Vinca Tablets below) were generally regarded as token or symbolic only however, following other discoveries with the same symbols in the region, it is now suspected that the Vinca script represents a proto-language similar to those from the Great civilisations that emerged a thousand years later in Egypt, The Middle East and in the Indus Valley.

Richard Rudgley proposed that the Old European script emerged from a system of symbolism rooted in the subconscious of the Neolithic. He said of it...

'Gimbutas proposed that it [the Old European Script] was part of a much wider corpus of signs that expressed cosmological and spiritual beliefs of the Neolithic age... Gimbautus believed that such designs were not merely decorative but were elements of an 'alphabet of the metaphysical'.  

The study of such symbols shows that as the ancient world drew inspiration from the Neolithic, so too were the first farming communities of this period drawing inspiration from the symbolic traditions of the hunter-gatherers who went before them, this finding is enforced by the work of Alexander Marshack, who documented the persistence of the zigzag motif in the stone age art of the Upper Palaeolithic period echoed in the Neolithic . The zigzag also appears among the old European signs, and its significance can be traced back to ancient Egypt where the zigzag Hieroglyph means water. Maria Gimbatus found clear parallels between symbols from different emerging scripts, suggests that the thread of writing can be traced back to the end of the ice age, suggesting that writing has been an art that has come and gone in several different forms throughout time. Various styles of zoomorphic and anthropomorphic figurines are hallmarks of the culture, as are the Vinca symbols, which some conjecture to be an early form of proto-writing. The Tartaria tablets refers to a group of three tablets, discovered in 1961 by archaeologist Nicolae Vlassa at a Neolithic site in the village of Tartaria (about 30 km (19 mi) from Alba Iulia), in Romania. Two of the tablets are rectangular and the third is round. They are all small, the round one being only 6 cm (2½ in) across, and two  - one round and one rectangular - have holes drilled through them. All three have symbols inscribed only on one face. The tablets, dated to around 5,300 BC, bear incised symbols - the Vinca symbols - and have been the subject of considerable controversy among archaeologists, some of whom claim that the symbols represent the earliest known form of writing in the world. subsequent radiocarbon dating on the Tartaria finds pushed the date of the tablets (and therefore of the whole Vinca culture) much further back, to as long ago as 5,500 BC, the time of the early Eridu phase of the Sumerian civilization in Mesopotamia. This finding has reversed our concept of the origin of writing, and it is now believed that the Sumerians inherited a Vinca tradition of 'magical' or 'meaningful' scripture, probably following the collapse of the Vinca homeland c. 3,500 BC. 

Similar motifs have been found on pots excavated at Gradeshnitsa in Bulgaria, Vinca in Serbia and a number of other locations in the southern Balkans. Ancient tablets found in South Bulgaria are written in the oldest European script found ever, German scientists say. The tablets, unearthed near the Southern town of Kardzhali, are nearly 7,000 years old, and bear the ancient script of the Cretan (Minoan) civilization, according to scientists from the University of Heidelberg, who examined the foundings. This is the Cretan writing, also known as Linear A script, which dates back to XV-XIV century B.C. The discovery proves the theory of the Bulgarian archaeologists that the script on the foundings is one of the oldest known to humankind, the archaeologist Nikolay Ovcharov announced Wednesday. Ovcharov, who is heading the archaeological expedition in the ancient Perperikon complex near Kardzhali, called the discovery “revolutionary”. It throws a completely different light on Bulgaria’s history, he said in an interview for the National Television.

title: IVC Religion In Iron Age Tamil Nadu By NGanesan 2016 16th WSC
description: Indus Crocodile Religion as seen in the Iron Age Tamil Nadu  Dr. Nagamanickam Ganesan Houston, Texas, USA Abstract:  This article is about some aspects of Indian religion in the Post-Harappan period providing a link to the Indus Valley Civilization seen in its Bronze Age seals. The meaning of the anthropomorphic axes found in the Indo-Gangetic doab plains of the Second Millennium BC as a ritual symbol of a Makara (crocodile) god will be presented. The characteristic fish sign pointing to the Dravidian language spoken by the elite Harappans has long been explored from the days of Fr. H. Heras, SJ. However, the importance of crocodiles in IVC culture is recently coming to light (A. Parpola, 2011). When this Crocodile cult disappears and gets forgotten in North India, it appears as large monolithic sculptures in the megalithic South. An interpretation of the Tamil Brahmi inscription at Tirupparaṅkuṉṟam, near the ancient Pandyan capital Madurai, discovered by History department, Pondicherry University will be offered as mentioning the crocodile god and his spouse. The Aśvamedha sacrifice on the banks of a Water Tank was performed for a crocodile as evidenced in Pāndyan Peruvaḻuti and Chera coins. Graffiti symbols from Sāṇūr and Sūlūr as linguistic sign for the crocodile deity, and the crocodile couple in Adichanallur burial urn (500 BCE) along with the battle-axe bearing great god in Sangam poetry will be used to illustrate the prevalence of the crocodile based religion until the Early Sangam period. The first stone sculpture made in south India at such places as Mottur, Udaiyarnatham, - monumental in size, over ten feet tall -, in the Iron Age will be linked to the earlier metallic Anthropomorphic Axes in the Yamuna-Gangetic doab, found in many Post-Harappan Ochre Colored Pottery sites of North India. This article will include etymology of Dravidian names such as Viṭaṅkar, Nakar, Ghaṛiāl, Makara, Karā for the three species of Indian crocodiles. Finally, an interpretation of Gudimallam Viṭaṅkar (Liṅgam) as Varuṇa, rather than as Śiva assumed by earlier scholars like A. K. Coomaraswamy, is offered. In the subsequent Pallava period, development of Tantric Śaivism includes the tantric term Viṭaṅkar applied more broadly for the forms of Śiva like naked Bhikṣāṭana and Somāskanda. This paper was published in the Proceedings of the 16th World Sanskrit Conference, held in Bangkok, Thailand, 2016.

title: The Decipherment of the Indus Script - "Stha" Excerpt
description: This excerpt from The Decipherment of the Indus Script by Jessica Scott Dunn presents a Sanskrit‑based interpretation of key Indus signs, showing that the bull’s shoulder‑mark functions as a ritual term tied to the Sanskrit root stha —“to stand, remain, be immovable.” Through iconographic and linguistic analysis, the text argues that this operator identifies the bull as a ritualized, immoveable deity and that related signs encode personal names and conditioned vowel behavior within a Sanskritic framework. This specific selection from the larger work offers a concise window into a much larger reconstruction situating the Indus script within an early Sanskrit ritual and linguistic Vedic system.

title: In Square Circle: Geometric Knowledge of the Indus Civilization
description: The earliest origins of mathematics in the Indian subcontinent is generally dated around 800-500 BCE when the {\em Sulbasutras} are thought to have been written. In this article we suggest that mathematical thinking in South Asia, in particular, geometry, may have had an even earlier beginning - in the third millenium BCE. We base our hypothesis on the analysis of design patterns, such as complex space-filling tiling, seen on artifacts of the Indus Valley Civilization (also referred to as the Mature Harappan Civilization, 2500-1900 BCE) which speaks of a deep understanding of sophisticated geometric principles.

It is a convergence, a point at which twelve distinct language systems, spanning three continents and four millennia, arrive independently at the same referent: a warrior people from the Caucasus-Caspian-Central Asian region who migrated to the Indian subcontinent and left their name inscribed in the landscape, literature, and lexicons of every civilization they touched. ​ The Turkic Gocer/Khazar, Persian Gurj, Georgian Kartveli/Gugark, Greek Iberia, Kurdish Goran, Arabic Jurjan, Chinese Kiu-che-lo, Russian Gruziya, Sanskrit Gurjara, Latin Georgia, and Armenian Virk are not competing etymologies. They are twelve windows into the same historical reality: a people whose warrior identity was so pronounced, so geographically extensive, and so historically durable that it survived every translation, every phonological shift, and every political transformation through which the ancient world passed. ​ The Gurjara-Pratihara Empire was not an anomaly. It was the culmination, the Indian expression of a warrior tradition that had already named the Caucasus, shaped the Median confederation, passed through the Zagros highlands, and left its signature on the roads, peaks, and fortresses of Kurdistan before it reached the plains of Rajasthan and Gujarat. The Gurjar nation did not merely pass through history. It made it.   ​ Parvez Dewan, surveying this same history from the perspective of Indian communities tracing their ancestry to Georgia, reaches a parallel conclusion: the Georgian-Khazar origin theory is not a marginal curiosity but a serious historical hypothesis supported by linguistic, cultural, material, and geographic evidence across multiple disciplines. He calls for comparative studies of material culture, livestock breeds, dress and ornaments, migration routes, historical records, and linguistic and archaeological evidence to carry this research forward. That agenda, fortified by both classical historical surveys and contemporary ethnic scholarship, constitutes the foundation upon which the next chapter of Gujjar historical scholarship must be built.   ​

title: Decoding Ancient Architecture and temples
description: This project presents an interdisciplinary study of the bronze figurine popularly known as the "Dancing Girl" of Mohenjo-daro through the traditional Indian Aayadi measurement system described in the classical literature of Vastu Shastra. Although the figurine has been extensively studied from archaeological, artistic, metallurgical, and cultural perspectives, its dimensions have not, to the best of the author's knowledge, been systematically examined using Aayadi metrology. The research applies Aayadi calculations to the published dimensions of the figurine and investigates possible relationships between its measurements, proportions, ornaments, and the derived Nakshatra. The study identifies an Aayadi Number of 3, which corresponds to Shatataraka according to the adopted methodology. It also examines numerical observations such as the approximate twenty-four bangles on the left arm and four bangles on the right arm as possible symbolic correspondences requiring further investigation. The observations presented in this study are proposed as research hypotheses rather than established historical conclusions. The primary objective of this project is to encourage interdisciplinary dialogue among archaeologists, historians, architects, Sanskrit scholars, metrologists, astronomers, and researchers of ancient Indian knowledge systems. The methodology, calculations, and supporting references are provided to facilitate independent evaluation, scholarly discussion, and future research into the possible role of traditional Indian metrology in the design and interpretation of archaeological artifacts. This study forms part of the author's continuing research on the Aayadi system, developed through more than seventeen years of investigation into ancient Indian architecture, sculpture, and traditional measurement principles.

title: The Essential Manu: Selections of verses from Sir William Jones' faithful rendering of the Manava Dharma Shastra, one of the most important ancient Indian legal treatises and summaries of the Vedas, into English. With an essay on the Saraswati River controversy and the dating of the perennial wisdom attributed to Manu
description: This paper, probably one of the first of its kind to be presented to the public in Europe and America since the days of Sir William Jones, Henry Thomas Colebrooke, Horace Heyman Wilson and Friedrich Max Müller, consists primarily in a partial and most painstaking digitization of the 1863 edition of the Lawbook of Manu, so-called, with Kulluka Bhatta's ancient, integrated gloss, as translated into English by Sir William Jones, as well as in commentary on the digitized passages, in which the striking parallels between parts of the Manava Dharma Shastra and two exceedingly famous and influential but very different literary works usually thought of as more or less “Western” in nature and origin, and as having no relation to ancient Indian or Vedic literature whatsoever. The two “Western” pieces of literature here referred to are Genesis, with its two creation stories and extensive genealogies, traditionally attributed to Moses, and Plato's singular study of human psychology and its relationship to the evolution and the fortunes of a society, the famous “Republic”. (“Western” is here used in a very loose and somewhat novel sense, of course, encompassing not only the so-called “Occident”, but also much of the region now styled the Middle East, a region once home to the Egyptian, the Hittite, the Phoenician and the Mesopotamian civilizations, for example, all of which exerted some influence on Greece and the rest of Europe, and which later became part of the rather fractured Greek Empire founded by Alexander, and then of the greater and more unified Roman Empire.) The facet of the greatest interest to Western researchers and scholars will likely prove to be the systematic comparison of certain features of the extensive creation story narrated by the Indian Manu (known as Swayambhuva/Svayambhuva Manu) to the two shorter “Biblical” creation accounts so familiar to most Westerners due to the inclusion of “the Pentateuch” in the category of Christian Holy Writ – a comparison which, for the sake of convenience, has been summarized in a table – while those primarily interested in metaphysics, or in ascertaining the Path to Spiritual Enlightenment and Wisdom, of which Plato's philosophy is one prominent manifestation, will probably find the subsequent parts of the abridged version of Manu's Laws, such as those taken from the chapter “On Transmigration and final Beatitude”, to be even more conducive to the rekindling of the Inner Fire. In addition to this, the reader will also, near the end of the paper, find a short discourse on “the Saraswati river controversy”, as one might call it, and on the bearing the ongoing discussion of the history and historicity of the Saraswati river has on another and equally contested issue, namely that of just how old the ancient Indian or Vedic literature – including, but not limited to, the Vedas – actually is. Whatever the eventual outcomes of these debates, it seems safe to say that the ancient high civilization now often spoken of as the Indus river valley civilization, or the Harappan civilization, is in fact partially, or perhaps even wholly, synonymous with the ancient Northern Indian or Vedic civilization which, according to the ancient Sanskrit texts and legends, was founded by Manu and the Great Sages, and of which both this legal treatise and the Ramayana epic poem and the Vedas speak, at great length. In other words, if Manu was, in some sense, the founder of the Indus valley civilization, or at least a part of it – whether he ever appeared on Earth or not – then there could hardly be an ancient literary work deserving of greater attention than the one attributed to him, since only two other civilizations in the recorded history of human kind, the ancient Egyptian and the Sumerian-Akkadian, can compete with the Harappan one, which some have proposed should be styled the Sindhu-Saraswati civilization instead, since the Saraswati river was at the very heart of its imagination.

description: Gharial god and Tiger goddess in the Indus valley, Some aspects of Bronze Age Indian Religion Dr. Naga Ganesan, Houston, TX, 2007 Abstract: In the Mature Harappan period seals and tablets produced about 4000 years ago, gharial crocodile is portrayed as a 'horned' being. As in the famous Pashupati seals (M-304), this horned gharial deity is the central figure surrounded by a typical set of animals. A female being, often connected with tigers, is seen coupling together with the gharial in a fecundity scene in an Indus Valley Civilization (IVC) creation myth. A number of seals show a man on the tree along with a tiger below. This shaman on the tree and tiger motif is linked archaeologically with the gharial deity in the sky, and the Mesopotamian Gilgamesh-like goddess shown between two tigers in IVC tablets and moulds. A comprehensive evaluation of the imagery recorded in the Indus glyptic art is needed to understand the pan-Indus founders' myth cycle, and it is illustrated with pictures of the IVC sealings. These religious myths of the gharial and tiger divinities are at least as important as the tree goddess worship in M-1186 with a shaman, markhor goat and seven women in front of a bodhi fig tree. title: 2024-12-03_Civilization #20： The Proto-Buddhists of the Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization
description: Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Indus Valley were the three great civilizations of the Bronze Age. What made the Indus Valley Civilization distinct? Why did they decline? What is their legacy? In this lecture to his Chinese high school students, Jiang Xueqin explains that the Indus Valley Civilization (also known as the Harappan Civilization) was mainly a peaceful and egalitarian society, which prospered because of its global trade networks. This civilization had standardized weights and measurements, sophisticated urban planning, as well as private indoor latrines. The dramatic climate change of the 4.2 kiloyear event caused Egypt’s Old Kingdom, Mesopotamia’s Akkadian empire, and the Indus Valley Civilization to decline. The Egyptians left us the Pyramids, the Mesopotamians left us the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the Harappans left us spiritual wealth. From the interaction with the Proto-Indo-Iranians, the Harappan civilization would eventually give birth to Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, which continue to give hope and meaning to billions of people today.

title: Mohenjo Daro Documentary
description: Mohenjo-daro  (means 'Mound of the Dead Men') is an archaeological site in the province of Sindh, Pakistan. Built around 2500 BCE, it was one of the largest settlements of the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation, and one of the world's earliest major cities, contemporaneous with the civilizations of ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Minoan Crete, and Norte Chico. Mohenjo-daro was abandoned in the 19th century BCE as the Indus Valley Civilization declined, and the site was not rediscovered until the 1920s. Significant excavation has since been conducted at the site of the city, which was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980. The site is currently threatened by erosion and improper restoration. Mohenjo-daro is located off the right (west) bank of the lower Indus river in Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan. It lies on a Pleistocene ridge in the flood plain of the Indus, around 28 kilometers (17 mi) from the town of Larkana. Mohenjo-daro was built in the 26th century BCE.  It was one of the largest cities of the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, also known as the Harappan Civilization which developed around 3,000 BCE from the prehistoric Indus culture. At its height, the Indus Civilization spanned much of what is now Pakistan and North India, extending westwards to the Iranian border, south to Gujarat in India and northwards to an outpost in Bactria, with major urban centers at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Mohenjo-daro was the most advanced city of its time, with remarkably sophisticated civil engineering and urban planning. When the Indus civilization went into sudden decline around 1900 BCE, Mohenjo-daro was abandoned. The ruins of the city remained undocumented for around 3,700 years until R. D. Banerji, an officer of the Archaeological Survey of India, visited the site in 1919–20 identifying what he thought to be a Buddhist stupa (150–500 CE) known to be there and finding a flint scraper which convinced him of the site's antiquity. This led to large-scale excavations of Mohenjo-daro led by K. N. Dikshit in 1924–25, and John Marshall in 1925–26.[15] In the 1930s major excavations were conducted at the site under the leadership of Marshall, D. K. Dikshitar and Ernest Mackay. Further excavations were carried out in 1945 by Mortimer Wheeler and his trainee, Ahmad Hasan Dani. The last major series of excavations were conducted in 1964 and 1965 by George F. Dales. After 1965 excavations were banned due to weathering damage to the exposed structures, and the only projects allowed at the site since have been salvage excavations, surface surveys, and conservation projects. In the 1980s, German and Italian survey groups led by Michael Jansen and Maurizio Tosi used less invasive archeological techniques, such as architectural documentation, surface surveys, and localized probing, to gather further information about Mohenjo-daro. A dry core drilling conducted in 2015 by Pakistan's National Fund for Mohenjo-daro revealed that the site is larger than the unearthed area.

title: HINDUSTANI SUPREME COURT JUDGEMENT ON HINDUISM
description: HINDUSTANI SUPREME COURT JUDGEMENT ON HINDUISM  ▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎▪︎ The Noahic and Persian/Non-Arab Background of Indian History          _________ ​A Study of Subcontinental Indigenous Population, Semitic & Ajami Migrations, and Ancient Religious Evolution            __________ ​Research & Editing: Abdul Rashid Bajar Gujjar            ____________ ​Introduction ​The history of humanity is not merely a chronicle of political empires or geographical boundaries; rather, it is a continuous journey of racial migrations, the blending of civilizations, and the formation and evolution of beliefs.  While the history of the Indian subcontinent is generally described through a localized cultural lens, a comparative study of ancient Semitic traditions, Iranian mythology, Vedic narratives, and Central Asian migrations connects this region to the ancient worlds of Mesopotamia, Persia, Greece, and the Caucasus. ​By consolidating these historical, mythological, and traditional narratives, this paper examines how the earliest population of the subcontinent was shaped by various civilizational waves and how the religious and intellectual influences of the ancient world migrated into India. ​1. The Post-Flood Resettlement of the Subcontinent       ________ ​According to ancient historical accounts, following the Great Flood of Prophet Noah (Noah's Ark), humanity was redistributed across different regions through the descendants of his three sons such as Shem (Sam), Ham, and Japheth (Yafith). Islamic, Judaic, and certain ancient Eastern traditions directly link the lineage of the subcontinent to these migratory patterns. ​The Tradition of Hind and Sindh ________ ​According to historians, the Indian subcontinent was repopulated after the Great Flood by Hazrat Hind and Hazrat Sindh (descendants in the patriarchal line). The first stop of this early settlement is said to have been near the mountain fortress of Aornos, which was later known as Wai Hind, Hind  or Hund. It is from this lineage that the Indus River (Sindhu/Sindh) and the land of India (Hind) derived their historical identities. ​Japhetic Migrations and Northern Routes     _______________ ​According to certain historical theories, Gomer, a descendant of Japheth, along with associated tribes, migrated from Central Asia, Turkestan, and the Tarim Basin, entering the subcontinent through the northern routes of the Himalayas. Some researchers connect these migrations to the early Indo-European displacements. ​2. Ancient Indian Traditions and the Eras of Ram Ji and Shiva Ji       ____________ ​Several historians present Ram Ji and Shiva Ji as ancient religious and cultural figures who existed centuries before the formal codification of modern Hinduism.  Certain historical perspectives link these figures to the ancient peoples of Iran, the Zagros Mountains, and Central Asia. ​Zagros and Ancient Eastern Connections         ____________ ​According to one theory, an ancient figure named "Dashratha or Draishith", who is attributed to the lineage of Kush bin Hind in some traditions, emerged in the mountainous regions of Zagros.  Later, the epics of Rama Ji and his lineage became intertwined with this cultural tradition. ​The Tradition of Luv and Kush. __________________ ​According to various traditions, the resettlement of India was spearheaded by Ram Ji’s sons, Luv and Kush, who established their religious  beliefs  across different regions of Northern India. ​3. Nimrod, Zahhak, and the Evolution of Idolatry in the Ancient World      ______________ ​In the traditions of the ancient Middle East, Nimrod is portrayed as a powerful monarch who claimed divinity and promoted celestial worship.  In the religious systems of Babylon, Egypt, and Mesopotamia, the worship of celestial bodies, deities, and symbolic idols occupied a central position. ​Nimrod and Babylon        ___________ ​According to Islamic and other historical accounts, Nimrod established a highly organized religious and political system in Babylon where idolatry received state patronage. This era later facilitated the spread of various polytheistic beliefs among Semitic and non-Semitic tribes. ​Zahhak and the Iranian Tradition ___________________ ​In Persian mythology, particularly in Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh, Zahhak is described as a tyrannical ruler and a "Second Nimrod."  According to the narrative, Fereydun and Kaveh the Blacksmith led a rebellion against him, defeating and imprisoning him in Mount Damavand. This legend is viewed in Iranian culture as a symbol of resistance against tyranny and polytheism. ​4. Religious Waves of Mesopotamia, Greece, and the Subcontinent    ________________ ​In the ancient world, Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Iran, and Greece served as major cultural and commercial hubs.  Various tribes periodically migrated from these regions toward Central Asia and the subcontinent. ​Some historians identify Javan (Yavan), Tubal, and Meshech as the progenitors of the Greek peoples, while Tubal and Meshech are categorized as tribes belonging to Anatolia and the Caucasus. The eastern interactions of these nations transmitted religious concepts, astrological beliefs, and mythological lore across various parts of Asia. ​Turan and Fereydun _________________ ​According to Iranian history, Fereydun’s son, Tur, established his rule over the regions of Central Asia. Certain traditions link Turan (extending toward modern Tehran/Turkestan), Transoxiana, and Northern India through ancient cultural ties. These historical records highlight elements of monotheism, reform, and the struggle against ancient polytheistic systems. ​5. The Decline of the Indus Valley and New Civilizational Formations _____________________ ​Archaeological evidence indicates that the Indus Valley Civilization gradually declined between approximately 1900 BC and 1500 BC. The causes of this decline are believed to include climate change, shifts in river courses, economic crises, and mass migrations. ​New Waves of Migration ____________________ ​Following the decline of the Indus Valley, new groups entered the subcontinent through the northwestern passes. These included Hindus,  Huns, Aryan tribes, Central Asian clans, and communities influenced by Western civilizations. They brought with them their languages, religions, astrological concepts, and mythological traditions, which were later recorded in the Rigveda and Puranas. ​Religious Evolution and Hinduism _____________________ ​The various3 civilizational waves arriving in the subcontinent blended with indigenous customs to form a complex religious and philosophical framework. In later eras, this evolutionary process manifested into the diverse forms of Hinduism through the synthesis of Vedic traditions, local beliefs, mythological epics, and philosophical schools. ​Conclusion ____________ ​The history of the Indian subcontinent is not merely a localized chronicle; it is an integral part of the grand migrations, cultural trends, and religious evolutions of the ancient world. Semitic traditions, Iranian mythology, Central Asian migrations, and Vedic narratives altogether construct a historical landscape where India emerges as a vital crossroads of ancient East-West connections. ​These traditions play a crucial role in understanding the collective memory, cultural identity, and civilizational consciousness of ancient peoples. In this context, the Noachian and Ajami background of Indian history invites a broader, inter-civilizational study. ​Alternative Historical Perspectives _____________ According to alternative historical theories, groups arriving from Mesopotamia, Khorasan, and Western Asia after 1500 BC played a foundational role in the religious and cultural synthesis of the subcontinent. Under these theories, it is asserted that specific concepts of idolatry migrated from Mesopotamia to the subcontinent, heavily influencing its subsequent religious evolution. Proponents of this view argue that these groups were not originally indigenous to India, but rather entered the land originally settled by Hazrat Hind from regions spanning Italy, Greece, Mesopotamia, and Khorasan. Hindustan Supreme Court and Hindus / Hindutva or Hinduvita _______________ ​Furthermore, according to rulings by the Supreme Court of India in 1966 and 1995, Hinduism is categorized not as a specific religion or ethnicity / communal group, but rather as a "way of life," as outlined in the legal judgments detailed below. ​1. Hinduism is a "Way of Life," Not a Religion ​On January 14, 1966, the Supreme Court of India, in Civil Appeal No. 517 of 1964 (AIR 1966 SC 1119; SCR (3) 242), titled "Sastri Yagnapurushadji and Others v. Muldas Bhudardas Vaishya and Another", a five-judge bench comprising Chief Justice P. B. Gajendragadkar, Justice K. N. Wanchoo, Justice M. Hidayatullah, Justice V. Ramaswami, and Justice P. Satyanarayana Raju, ruled: ​"Hindu religion does not claim any one prophet; it does not worship any one God; it does not subscribe to any one dogma; it does not believe in any one philosophic concept; it does not follow any one set of religious rites or performances; in fact, it does not appear to satisfy the narrow traditional features of any religion or creed. It may broadly be described as a way of life and nothing more." ​2. The Definition of Hindutva and Hinduism ​On December 11, 1995, in Civil Appeal No. 2835 of 1989, titled "Dr. Ramesh Yeshwant Prabhoo v. Shri Prabhakar Kashinath Kunte and Others", a three-judge bench consisting of Justice J. S. Verma, Justice N. P. Singh, and Justice K. Venkataswami, mirrored this stance and clarified that Hindutva and Hinduism signify a "way of life" and the state of mind of the people of the region, and are not to be understood as a rigid, dogmatic religion. ​Those who propagate narrow definitions of the term "Hindu" are urged to study these landmark judgments of the Supreme Court of India.       ••••••••••••••••••• ​Societal Structure of the Indus Valley Civilization ___________________ ​In Harappan society, women were free to develop their individual talents and personal choices without institutional boundaries. Rather than being treated as mere property, historical sculptures discovered across the Indus Valley indicate that women held an incredibly prestigious status, often viewed as central, or even superior, to their male counterparts due to their authority over domestic, societal, and spiritual domains. ​While men primarily managed the agrarian economy and the foundational functionality of Harappan governance, women played an equally vital role in cultural and logistical spheres, including active roles in local transportation and regional activities across the river valleys.  Ultimately, the social fabric of the Indus Valley Civilization was built upon a profound equilibrium, where men and women enjoyed equal amounts of mutual respect across social, economic, and cultural وابستہ قبائل وسطی ایشیا، ترکستان، اور ٹیرم بیسن سے ہوتے ہوئے ہمالیہ کے شمالی راستوں کے ذریعے برصغیر میں داخل ہوئے۔ ان ہجرتوں کو بعض محققین ابتدائی ہند۔یورپی (Indo-European) نقل مکانی سے بھی جوڑتے ہیں۔ بعض تاریخی نظریات ان شخصیات کو ایران، زاگروس، اور وسطی ایشیا کی قدیم اقوام سے بھی جوڑتے ہیں۔ زاگروس اور قدیم مشرقی روابط ایک نظریے کے مطابق “دریشتھ” نامی قدیم شخصیت، جو بعض روایات میں کوش بن ہند کی title: Usage Of Mortar In Some Of The Major Harappan Sites
description: Abstract The term ‘Mortar' means bonding materials, mainly used for joining the stones or bricks of an architectural monument or structure. It is mainly the mixture or amalgamation of lime, sand, and water as needed. Although experts believe that the Harappan Civilization period was the beginning of using mortar for bonding purposes and plastering in the Indian subcontinent. From that period onwards, the use of mortar has been used very widely. Archaeological excavations and remains give us several examples of this material. Apart from archaeological evidence, ancient Indian literature also helps us to reveal more about mortar. Vedic and Later Vedic texts and a large number of Sanskrit texts of the ancient and early medieval period, Shilpashastras, and some Buddhist texts also mentioned the mortar. In textual evidence, the terms Sudha and Vajralepa have also been used as mortar. This article’s main focus will be on the mortar used in some archaeological sites of the Indus Valley civilization only.

title: The ancient Indus : urbanism, economy, and society
description: xix, 396 p. : 23 cm

Overview: This early civilization was erased from human memory until 1924, when it was rediscovered and announced in the Illustrated London Times. Our understanding of the Indus has been partially advanced by textual sources from Mesopotamia that contains references to Meluhha, a land identified by cuneiform specialists as the Indus, with which the ancient Mesopotamians traded and engaged in battles. In this volume, Rita P. Wright uses both Mesopotamian texts but principally the results of archaeological excavations and surveys to draw a rich account of the Indus civilization's well-planned cities, its sophisticated alterations to the landscape, and the complexities of its agrarian and craft-producing economy. She focuses principally on the social networks established between city and rural communities; farmers, pastoralists, and craft producers; and Indus merchants and traders and the symbolic imagery that the civilization shared with contemporary cultures in Iran, Mesopotamia, Central Asia, and the Persian Gulf region. Broadly comparative, her study emphasizes the interconnected nature of early societies

title: The Roots of Hinduism : The Early Aryans and the Indus Civilization
description: xvi, 363 pages : 26 cm

"Hinduism has two major roots. The more familiar is the religion brought to South Asia in the second millennium BCE by speakers of Aryan or Indo-Iranian languages, a branch of the Indo-European language family. Another, more enigmatic, root is the Indus civilization of the third millennium BCE, which left behind exquisitely carved seals and thousands of short inscriptions in a long-forgotten pictographic script. Discovered in the valley of the Indus River in the early 1920s, the Indus civilization had a population estimated at one million people, in more than 1000 settlements, several of which were cities of some 50,000 inhabitants. With an area of nearly a million square kilometers, the Indus civilization was more extensive than the contemporaneous urban cultures of Mesopotamia and Egypt. Yet, after almost a century of excavation and research the Indus civilization remains little understood. How might we decipher the Indus inscriptions? What language did the Indus people speak? What deities did they worship? Asko Parpola has spent fifty years researching the roots of Hinduism to answer these fundamental questions, which have been debated with increasing animosity since the rise of Hindu nationalist politics in the 1980s. In this pioneering book, he traces the archaeological route of the Indo-Iranian languages from the Aryan homeland north of the Black Sea to Central, West, and South Asia. His new ideas on the formation of the Vedic literature and rites and the great Hindu epics hinge on the profound impact that the invention of the horse-drawn chariot had on Indo-Aryan religion. Parpola's comprehensive assessment of the Indus language and religion is based on all available textual, linguistic and archaeological evidence, including West Asian sources and the Indus script. The results affirm cultural and religious continuity to the present day and, among many other things, shed new light on the prehistory of the key Hindu goddess Durga and her Tantric cult"--

"This pioneering study derives Hinduism from the traditions brought to South Asia by Aryan-speaking pastoralists from the Eurasian steppes and those of the Indus Civilization, reconstructed from its visual and inscriptional remains and from West Asian and classical/modern South Asian sources"--
